title: The monk who spoke about war and race
hookLine: from the cloister he wrote letters against nuclear war and for civil rights
last: A SMALL HOUSE IN THE WOODS.

cards: The early 1960s. Families are building fallout shelters in their backyards. Schoolkids practice hiding under their desks in case of a nuclear bomb.
In the South, people marching for civil rights are being beaten on the evening news.
And in a silent monastery in Kentucky, a monk is typing letter after letter to anyone who'll listen: this is wrong, and Christians should say so. Some people were grateful. Some were furious.
Some told him monks should stay out of it.

teach.b: First, war. In 1961 and 1962, Merton wrote what he called the Cold War Letters, to friends, scholars and activists, arguing that nuclear war could never be squared with the Gospel.

When he tried to publish on the subject, his order's superior general told him to stop. Merton obeyed and didn't publish that book. But he kept writing to friends, and the letters were copied and passed from hand to hand.

In 1963, Pope John XXIII issued Pacem in Terris, Peace on Earth, a letter to the whole world calling for an end to the arms race. Merton felt the Church had said out loud what he'd been told to keep quiet. Third, race.

In essays collected in 1964, including one called Letters to a White Liberal, Merton wrote that racism was a sickness of the whole society, not just a Southern problem, and that white Christians had to listen to Black Americans rather than tell them to wait.
Later that year he hosted a small retreat at Gethsemani for peace activists, to pray about what faith asked of them. Fourth, the root.
Merton said this came from contemplation, not from politics. Years before, on a Louisville street corner, he had seen every stranger shining. You can't see that and then shrug at a bomb or a beating.

Jesus said, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." And Paul: "you are all one in Christ Jesus." For Merton, silence wasn't the opposite of speaking up.
It was where the words came from.

how: Catholic teaching on peace and human dignity runs through papal letters like Pacem in Terris (1963), and many Catholic peace and justice groups trace their inspiration in part to Merton's writing.

games.q: you're a monk who's written against nuclear war, and your superior tells you to stop publishing on it. what do you do?
o: obey, and keep writing letters to friends
games.why: Merton obeyed the ban on publishing, but his letters circulated hand to hand. in 1963 Pacem in Terris called for an end to the arms race.

practice: Bring to mind one place where people are hurting right now: a war in the news, a neighborhood, a family feud, a friend treated unfairly.

Don't argue about it in your head; just look at the people there as Merton did on that street corner, shining, and let one sentence come, something you could say or write for peace. If you pray, you can pray for them first.

wordCard.voice: Peacemakers, the word from the Gospel Merton lived out: writing against nuclear war and for civil rights from the quiet of his monastery. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: peace on earth, the title of John XXIII's 1963 letter.
